en.title: The Full Cup
en.body:
A scholar travelled far to ask a tea master about Zen. Before the master could say a word, the scholar began explaining everything he already knew.

The master listened quietly and started to pour tea. The cup filled, then overflowed, and the tea ran across the table and onto the floor.

“Stop!” cried the scholar. “The cup is full!”

“Like this cup,” said the master, “you are full of your own ideas. How can I show you anything, unless you first empty your cup?”
questions: What am I holding so tightly that nothing new can find room?
Where in today could I leave a little empty space — at the table, or in a conversation?

zh-Hant.title: 滿杯的茶
zh-Hant.body:
有位學者遠道而來，向一位茶師請教禪。茶師還沒開口，學者已經滔滔不絕，說著自己早就知道的一切。

茶師靜靜聽著，然後開始倒茶。茶杯滿了，茶水溢出來，流過桌面，滴到地上。

「別倒了！」學者喊道，「杯子已經滿了！」

「就像這只杯子，」茶師說，「你心裡也裝滿了自己的想法。除非你先把杯子倒空，我又怎麼能給你看見什麼呢？」
questions: 我正緊緊握著什麼，以致新的東西沒有地方進來？
今天有哪一刻——在餐桌上，或在一場談話裡——我可以留一點空白？

en.title: Stone Soup
en.body:
A weary traveller came to a village where every door stayed shut. Nobody had food to spare, they said.

He lit a small fire in the square, set down a pot of water, and dropped in a smooth stone. “Stone soup,” he told the curious faces at the windows. “It only needs a little something extra.”

One neighbour brought a carrot. Another brought potatoes, another barley, another a handful of herbs. Each thought, surely one small thing won’t matter.

By evening the whole village sat together around one pot, and there was more than enough for everyone.
questions: What small thing could I add to someone’s table this week?
When has a meal become more than any one of us brought to it?

zh-Hant.title: 石頭湯
zh-Hant.body:
一位疲憊的旅人來到一座村子，家家戶戶門都緊閉。村民都說，自己沒有多餘的食物。

他在廣場上生起一小堆火，架起一鍋水，丟進一顆光滑的石頭。「石頭湯，」他對窗後好奇的臉孔說，「只差一點點配料就好了。」

一位鄰居拿來一根胡蘿蔔，另一位帶來馬鈴薯，有人加了大麥，有人放進一把香草。每個人都想：這麼一點點，應該不礙事。

到了傍晚，整個村子的人圍坐在同一口鍋旁，湯多得足夠每個人吃飽。
questions: 這個星期，我可以為誰的餐桌添上一點什麼？
有沒有哪一餐，因為大家各自帶來一點，而變得比任何一個人帶的都豐盛？

en.title: The Long Chopsticks
en.body:
A traveller was once shown two great banquet halls. In each, a table was heaped with wonderful food, and every guest held chopsticks longer than their arms.

In the first hall, people were thin and unhappy. They stretched and struggled, but could not bring the food to their own mouths.

In the second hall, the food was just the same and so were the chopsticks. But here everyone was smiling and full. Each person simply used their long chopsticks to feed the person across the table.
questions: Who could I feed today, in whatever way, so that we are both nourished?
Where am I struggling alone with something that would be lighter if shared?

zh-Hant.title: 長長的筷子
zh-Hant.body:
有位旅人被帶去看兩間大宴會廳。兩間廳裡都擺滿了美味的菜餚，每位客人手中的筷子，都比自己的手臂還要長。

第一間廳裡，人人面黃肌瘦、愁眉不展。他們伸長手臂，拚命努力，卻怎麼也沒辦法把食物送進自己的嘴裡。

第二間廳裡，菜餚一樣，筷子也一樣。可是這裡的人個個面帶笑容、吃得飽足。因為每個人都用長長的筷子，夾菜餵給對面的人。
questions: 今天我可以用什麼方式餵養誰，讓彼此都得到滋養？
有什麼事我正獨自苦撐，其實分擔出去會輕鬆許多？

en.title: Maybe
en.body:
An old farmer’s horse ran away. “Such bad luck!” said the neighbours. “Maybe,” said the farmer.

A few days later the horse returned, leading a herd of wild horses. “Such good luck!” said the neighbours. “Maybe,” said the farmer.

His son tried to ride one of the wild horses, fell, and broke his leg. “Such bad luck!” “Maybe,” said the farmer.

Then soldiers came to the village to take away every young man, but they passed over the boy with the broken leg.

The farmer went on tending his fields, tasting what each day brought.
questions: What recent event have I judged too quickly as good or bad?
What would change in me if I answered a hard day with “maybe”?

zh-Hant.title: 也許吧
zh-Hant.body:
一位老農夫的馬跑掉了。鄰居說：「真倒楣！」農夫說：「也許吧。」

幾天後，那匹馬回來了，還帶回一群野馬。鄰居說：「真幸運！」農夫說：「也許吧。」

他的兒子騎上一匹野馬，摔了下來，跌斷了腿。鄰居說：「真倒楣！」農夫說：「也許吧。」

後來軍隊來到村裡，要把所有的年輕人帶走，卻因為那孩子的腿斷了，沒有帶他。

農夫依舊照顧他的田地，細細品嚐每一天帶來的滋味。
questions: 最近有哪件事，我太快就斷定是好或是壞？
面對艱難的一天，如果我回答「也許吧」，我會有什麼不同？

en.title: Is That So?
en.body:
A Zen teacher named Hakuin lived quietly in his village, and everyone respected him. One day a young woman in the village was found to be with child. Under pressure from her angry parents she named Hakuin as the father.

The parents stormed to his door. “Is that so?” was all he said.

When the child was born, they brought the baby to him, and he cared for it lovingly, though his good name was gone.

A year later the young woman confessed that the real father was a boy from the market. The parents came back, full of shame, and asked for the child.

“Is that so?” said Hakuin, and gave the baby back.
questions: When did I last defend myself, when I could have let it rest?
What would it feel like to meet both praise and blame with the same calm?

zh-Hant.title: 是這樣嗎？
zh-Hant.body:
白隱禪師安靜地住在村子裡，人人都敬重他。有一天，村裡一位年輕女子被發現懷了孕。在憤怒的父母逼問之下，她說孩子的父親是白隱。

父母怒氣沖沖地闖到他門前。他只說了一句：「是這樣嗎？」

孩子出生後，他們把嬰兒送來給他，他滿心疼愛地照顧著，儘管名聲早已一落千丈。

一年後，那位女子坦白，真正的父親是市場裡的一個少年。父母羞愧萬分地回來，求他把孩子還給他們。

白隱說：「是這樣嗎？」便把孩子交還了。
questions: 我上一次為自己辯解，是在什麼時候？那時其實可以放下嗎？
如果我能以同樣的平靜面對讚美與責難，那會是什麼感覺？

en.title: The Mustard Seed
en.body:
Kisa Gotami’s young child had died, and in her grief she carried him from door to door, begging for medicine that could bring him back.

At last someone sent her to the Buddha. “I can help,” he said gently. “Bring me a handful of mustard seed, from a home where no one has ever died.”

She set out hopeful. But at every door people said, “We have lost a father,” or “a sister,” or “a friend.”

As evening came she understood: she was not alone in her sorrow. Every household knew it. And with that understanding, she was finally able to lay her child to rest.
questions: Whose sorrow could I sit beside today, without trying to fix it?
When someone shared their loss with me, what did they most need?

zh-Hant.title: 芥菜籽
zh-Hant.body:
吉沙喬達彌年幼的孩子過世了。悲痛之中，她抱著孩子一家一家地敲門，乞求能讓他復活的藥。

最後有人指點她去見佛陀。「我能幫你，」佛陀溫和地說，「請你從一戶從來沒有人去世過的人家，帶一把芥菜籽來給我。」

她滿懷希望地出發，但每一戶人家都說：「我們失去了父親。」「我們失去了姊妹。」「我們失去了朋友。」

傍晚時分，她終於明白：自己並不是唯一悲傷的人，家家戶戶都懂得這種痛。有了這份明白，她才終於能讓孩子安息。
questions: 今天我可以陪誰坐一坐、守著他的悲傷，而不急著去替他解決？
當有人向我訴說失去，他最需要的是什麼？

en.title: The Cracked Pot
en.body:
A water carrier had two pots, which hung from either end of a pole across his shoulders. One was perfect. The other had a crack, and every day it arrived home half empty.

After two years the cracked pot felt ashamed. “I am sorry,” it said. “I leak all the way home, and you get so little water for all your work.”

The carrier smiled. “Look at the path as we walk back.”

On the pot’s side of the path, wildflowers grew all along the way. “I have always known about your crack,” he said. “So I planted seeds on your side. Every day you have watered them.”
questions: What do I see as my flaw that might also be quietly watering something?
Whose “cracks” could I look at differently today?

zh-Hant.title: 有裂縫的水壺
zh-Hant.body:
有個挑水的人，扁擔兩頭各掛著一只水壺。一只完好無缺，另一只有一道裂縫，每天回到家時，水都只剩一半。

過了兩年，有裂縫的水壺覺得很羞愧。「對不起，」它說，「我一路漏水，讓你辛苦一場，卻只挑回這麼一點點水。」

挑水人笑了笑：「回程的路上，你看看路邊。」

在水壺這一側的小路旁，野花一路盛開。「我早就知道你有裂縫，」他說，「所以我在你這一邊撒下花種。每天，都是你在替它們澆水。」
questions: 我視為缺點的地方，是否也正悄悄滋養著什麼？
今天，我可以用不同的眼光看待誰的「裂縫」？

en.title: Wash Your Bowl
en.body:
A young monk came to the master Zhaozhou. “I have just arrived at the monastery,” he said. “Please teach me.”

“Have you eaten your porridge?” asked Zhaozhou.

“Yes, I have.”

“Then wash your bowl.”

At that moment, they say, the young monk understood. The teaching was not somewhere far away. It lived in the plain, next task in front of him.
questions: What is the simple next thing in front of me right now?
How would washing a bowl change if I gave it my whole attention?

zh-Hant.title: 洗缽去
zh-Hant.body:
一位年輕的僧人來見趙州禪師。「我剛入寺，」他說，「請師父指點。」

趙州問：「吃過粥了嗎？」

「吃過了。」

「那就洗缽去吧。」

據說，就在那一刻，年輕的僧人開悟了。教導並不在遠方，它就在眼前最平凡的下一件事裡。
questions: 此刻，我面前最簡單的下一件事是什麼？
如果我用全部的心力洗一只碗，這件事會有什麼不同？

en.title: The Old Cook and the Mushrooms
en.body:
Long ago, a young monk named Dōgen was visiting a port in China when he saw an elderly monk, the cook of a great monastery, walking a long way to buy mushrooms. Then, in the burning noon sun, the old man spread the mushrooms out to dry, his back bent and sweat running down his face.

“Why not let a younger person do this?” asked Dōgen. “Or wait until it is cooler?”

“Others are not me,” the cook replied. “How can what they do be my practice?”

“But why now, in this heat?”

“If not now,” said the old cook, “then when?”
questions: What is mine to do, and that I keep handing to someone else or to “later”?
Where could ordinary work in my day become a kind of practice?

zh-Hant.title: 老典座與香菇
zh-Hant.body:
很久以前，年輕的道元禪師造訪中國的一個港口，看見一位年長的僧人——一座大寺院的典座（掌廚的僧人）——走了很遠的路去買香菇。到了正午，烈日當空，老人彎著背，滿頭大汗，把香菇一一攤開曬乾。

道元問：「為什麼不請年輕人來做呢？或者等天涼一點再曬？」

老典座回答：「別人不是我。他們做的事，怎麼會是我的修行？」

「可是為什麼偏偏是現在、這樣的大太陽下？」

老典座說：「不是現在，更待何時？」
questions: 有什麼事本來是我該做的，我卻一直交給別人，或拖到「以後」？
我一天中平凡的工作，可以在哪裡變成一種修行？

en.title: Sujata’s Bowl
en.body:
After years of fasting, the seeker who would become the Buddha was so weak he could hardly sit upright beneath a tree.

A young woman named Sujata, who had made a promise to the tree spirit, came carrying a golden bowl of milk-rice. Seeing the thin figure under the branches, she thought he must be the spirit himself, and offered it with both hands.

He accepted, and ate slowly. Strength returned to his body, and his mind grew clear and steady.

One simple bowl, freely given, became part of the road to awakening.
questions: Who offered me nourishment at the moment I most needed it?
What would it mean to receive kindness without feeling I must earn it?

zh-Hant.title: 善生女的缽
zh-Hant.body:
經過多年苦修禁食，這位後來成為佛陀的修行者，身體虛弱得幾乎無法在樹下端坐。

有位名叫善生的年輕女子，曾向樹神許過願，捧著一只盛著乳糜的金缽前來。她看見樹下那瘦削的身影，以為他就是樹神，便雙手恭敬地獻上。

他接受了，慢慢地吃。力氣回到身上，心也變得清明而安定。

一缽簡單、無所求的供養，成了走向覺醒之路的一部分。
questions: 在我最需要的時候，是誰給了我養分？
如果我能接受善意，而不覺得非得「賺取」，那會是什麼樣子？

en.title: Burnt Rice
en.body:
Every time Grandmother made rice, a thin golden crust burned onto the bottom of the pot. She was embarrassed by it, and always apologised.

But the children kept coming to the kitchen just when the pot was almost empty. They scraped the crackling layer with spoons, arguing over who got the biggest piece, and it was the best part of dinner.

“The burnt part?” Grandmother laughed one evening, and stopped apologising for good.

Sometimes what we call a mistake is just something we haven’t yet learned to enjoy.
questions: What have I apologised for that someone else quietly treasured?
What “burnt rice” in my life could I try tasting differently?

zh-Hant.title: 鍋巴
zh-Hant.body:
每次奶奶煮飯，鍋底總會燒出一層薄薄的金黃色鍋巴。她覺得不好意思，總是連聲道歉。

可是孩子們每次都會在鍋子快見底的時候，跑到廚房來。他們拿著湯匙刮那層酥脆的鍋巴，吵著誰分到的最大塊——那是整頓晚餐裡最好吃的部分。

「燒焦的部分？」有天晚上奶奶笑了起來，從此再也不道歉了。

有時候，我們稱作「失誤」的東西，只是還沒學會去欣賞而已。
questions: 有什麼事我曾為它道歉，別人卻悄悄珍惜著？
我生活中有哪一份「鍋巴」，可以試著換個方式品嚐？

en.title: One Tomato
en.body:
Mei-Lin held a single tomato in her hand at the market, and suddenly wondered how it had got there.

Someone had saved the seed. Someone had planted it and watered it through long weeks. Rain had fallen, and the sun had come and gone. Someone had picked it gently, someone had packed it, someone had driven through the early dark to bring it here, and someone had set it on this stall.

She paid for the tomato, but stood a moment longer, quietly aware of everything she couldn’t pay for.

That evening she sliced it slowly, and it tasted like all those hands.
questions: Whose hands are in what I’ll eat today?
How could I thank the unseen people behind ordinary things?

zh-Hant.title: 一顆番茄
zh-Hant.body:
美琳在市場裡拿起一顆番茄，忽然好奇：它是怎麼來到這裡的？

有人留下了種子，有人把它種下，在漫長的幾個星期裡一次次澆水。雨落了，太陽升起又落下。有人輕輕摘下它，有人把它裝箱，有人在清晨的黑暗裡開車載運，又有人把它擺上這個攤位。

她付了番茄的錢，卻多站了一會兒，靜靜地意識到：有太多東西，是她付不起的。

那天晚上，她慢慢地把番茄切開，吃起來有著許許多多雙手的味道。
questions: 我今天要吃的東西裡，有誰的雙手？
我可以怎樣感謝平凡事物背後那些看不見的人？

en.title: The Smallest Pear
en.body:
When Kong Rong was four years old, a basket of pears was brought to the house, and his father told the children to help themselves.

The little boy walked past the big, shiny pears and chose the smallest one in the basket.

“Why that one?” his father asked, surprised.

“I am the youngest,” said the boy, “so the smallest pear is for me. The bigger ones belong to my older brothers.”

People in China have told this story for nearly two thousand years, because a child’s small gesture showed something the whole household understood: love is made of many small choices at the table.
questions: When did someone leave the bigger piece for me?
What small choice could show care for someone at my table today?

zh-Hant.title: 孔融讓梨
zh-Hant.body:
孔融四歲那年，家裡送來一籃梨子，父親讓孩子們自己挑選。

小男孩走過那些又大又亮的梨子，挑了籃子裡最小的一顆。

父親驚訝地問：「為什麼挑那一顆？」

孩子說：「我年紀最小，小的梨子該是我的。大的要留給哥哥們。」

這個故事在中國流傳了將近兩千年，因為孩子這一個小小的舉動，讓全家人都懂得：愛，是由餐桌上一個又一個小小的選擇組成的。
questions: 有沒有人曾經把較大的那一份留給我？
今天，我可以做出什麼小小的選擇，向餐桌旁的人表達關心？
